kcet|Chemistry|2012|11||0|0.s:
By Gay-Lussac's law, gas volumes at the same temperature and pressure react in the ratio of
the coefficients.
CH₄ + 2O₂ ⇒ CO₂ + 2H₂O
Oxygen needed for 20 ml of methane = 2 × 20 = 40 ml
Oxygen supplied = 50 ml, so 50 − 40 = 10 ml of O₂ is left over.
Carbon dioxide formed = 20 ml (1 : 1 with methane).
Water formed = 40 ml of vapour — but the question says the mixture is **cooled to room
temperature**, so the water condenses to a liquid and takes up no measurable gas volume.
That is the whole point of the cooling, and the step most often missed.
Gas remaining = unused O₂ + CO₂ = 10 + 20 = 30 ml
∴ 30 ml.

kcet|Chemistry|2012|12||0|0.s:
Neutralisation converts the acid completely to its sodium salt:
CH₃COOH + NaOH ⇒ CH₃COONa + H₂O
moles of acetic acid = 0.100 L × 0.1 mol L⁻¹ = 0.01 mol
so 0.01 mol of sodium acetate is formed.
Electrolysing that salt is Kolbe's reaction. Two acetate ions are discharged at the anode, each
losing CO₂, and the two methyl radicals couple:
2CH₃COO⁻ ⇒ 2CH₃• + 2CO₂ + 2e⁻ ⇒ C₂H₆ + 2CO₂ + 2e⁻
Note the 2 : 1 ratio — **two** acetates give **one** ethane:
moles of ethane = 0.01 / 2 = 0.005 mol
Volume at STP = 0.005 × 22400 = 112 ml
Forgetting the factor of two gives 224 ml, which is option (3).
∴ 112 ml.

kcet|Chemistry|2012|13||0|0.s:
Saccharin is an artificial sweetener, about 550 times as sweet as sucrose, and it passes
through the body unchanged — which is why it is used by diabetics.
It is manufactured from **toluene**. The route is:
toluene is sulphonated at the ortho position, the sulphonic acid is converted to the sulphonyl
chloride, treated with ammonia to give the sulphonamide, and the methyl group is then
oxidised to –COOH, which closes the ring onto the nitrogen to form the cyclic imide.
The benzene ring of saccharin comes straight from the toluene, and so does the carbon of its
carbonyl group — it is the original methyl, oxidised.
Cellulose and starch are carbohydrates and are not used here, and cyclohexane has no aromatic
ring to supply.
∴ toluene.

kcet|Chemistry|2012|17||0|0.s:
Compare experiments in pairs, changing one concentration at a time.
Experiments 1 and 2 — [A] is held at 0.2 while [B] doubles from 0.2 to 0.4:
rate goes 2 ⇒ 4, a factor of 2
2 = 2^y ⇒ y = 1, so the reaction is **first order in B**.
Experiments 2 and 3 — [B] is held at 0.4 while [A] triples from 0.2 to 0.6:
rate goes 4 ⇒ 36, a factor of 9
9 = 3^x ⇒ x = 2, so the reaction is **second order in A**.
Putting them together:
rate = k[A]²[B]
Overall order = 2 + 1 = 3.
Check with experiment 1: k = 2/((0.2)² × 0.2) = 2/0.008 = 250, and experiment 3 gives
250 × 0.36 × 0.4 = 36 ✓
∴ r = k[A]²[B].

kcet|Chemistry|2012|21||0|0.s:
The orbitals available in a shell are fixed by the quantum numbers.
For a principal quantum number n, the azimuthal quantum number l can take values
l = 0, 1, 2, … , (n − 1)
and those map to the letters s, p, d, f.
So shell n can contain only the first n types of orbital:
n = 1 ⇒ l = 0 only ⇒ 1s
n = 2 ⇒ l = 0, 1 ⇒ 2s, 2p
n = 3 ⇒ l = 0, 1, 2 ⇒ 3s, 3p, 3d — and no more
n = 4 ⇒ l = 0, 1, 2, 3 ⇒ 4s, 4p, 4d, 4f
An f orbital needs l = 3, which requires n ≥ 4. So **3f** cannot exist.
The others are all allowed: 2s (n=2, l=0), 2p (n=2, l=1) and 4d (n=4, l=2) ✓
∴ 3f is not possible.

kcet|Chemistry|2012|22||0|0.s:
Convert the volume to mass, then to moles, then count electrons.
mass = volume × density = 18 ml × 1 g ml⁻¹ = 18 g
Molar mass of water = 18 g mol⁻¹, so
moles = 18 / 18 = 1 mol
Now count the electrons in one molecule of H₂O:
2 hydrogens × 1 electron = 2
1 oxygen × 8 electrons = 8
total = 10 electrons per molecule
Total electrons = 1 mol × 6.022 × 10²³ molecules × 10 electrons
= 6.022 × 10²⁴
The factor of ten is what moves the exponent from 23 to 24; option (1) is the answer if you
count molecules instead of electrons.
∴ 6.02 × 10²⁴.

kcet|Chemistry|2012|23||0|0.s:
Hydrogen adds across the C=C double bonds of the unsaturated fatty acid chains, so the moles
of H₂ taken up equal the number of double bonds per molecule of oil.
That quantity is measured as the **iodine value** — the higher it is, the more unsaturated the
oil and the more hydrogen it absorbs.
Typical iodine values:
Linseed oil 170–204 ← highest, rich in linolenic acid with three C=C per chain
Sunflower seed oil 125–145
Mustard oil 95–125
Groundnut oil 85–100
Linseed oil is the most unsaturated of the four, which is also why it is a **drying** oil: those
double bonds cross-link on exposure to air, which is why it is used in paints and varnishes.
∴ linseed oil.

kcet|Chemistry|2012|24||0|0:
Sodium reacts violently with water:
2Na + 2H₂O ⇒ 2NaOH + H₂
The reaction is so exothermic that the hydrogen often ignites, and the metal skates about on
the surface because it is less dense than water.
Amalgamating the sodium — dissolving it in mercury — dilutes it. The sodium atoms are
dispersed through the mercury, so only a small fraction of the surface is sodium at any moment.
The reaction still proceeds, but steadily and controllably, which is why sodium amalgam is used
as a mild reducing agent in the laboratory.
The others do not work:
(1) Lowering the temperature only slows it slightly; sodium reacts even with ice.
(2) Sodium reacts with alcohol too, giving sodium ethoxide and hydrogen.
(4) Adding acetic acid makes it **more** vigorous, since sodium reacts faster with acid than
with water.
∴ amalgamating the sodium.

kcet|Chemistry|2012|25||0|0.s:
Osmotic pressure is a colligative property: π = iCRT, so it depends on the **number** of
dispersed particles, not their size.
In a colloid each particle is an aggregate containing thousands of molecules or atoms. So for a
given mass of dispersed material there are far fewer particles than there would be in a true
solution of the same mass.
Fewer particles means a much smaller molar concentration, and therefore a **low** osmotic
pressure.
It is not zero (3) — colloidal particles cannot pass a semipermeable membrane, so they do exert
a measurable pressure. That pressure is small but reliable enough to be used to determine the
molar masses of polymers and proteins.
The same reasoning explains why colloids show negligible elevation of boiling point and
depression of freezing point.
∴ low osmotic pressure.

kcet|Chemistry|2012|26||0|0.s:
Artificial rain is made by cloud seeding. Supercooled water droplets in a cloud need a
**nucleus** on which to crystallise; without one they stay liquid well below 0 °C and no rain falls.
Silver iodide works because its crystal lattice is almost identical to that of ice — both are
hexagonal, with lattice spacings differing by only about 1.5%.
A water molecule arriving at an AgI crystal therefore finds itself in very nearly the
arrangement it would adopt in ice, so ice grows on it readily. The AgI acts as a template, and
ice formation begins at about −4 °C instead of −40 °C.
The crystals grow, become heavy and fall, melting on the way down to give rain.
Being easy to spray (1) or insoluble (4) are convenient but incidental; the structural match is
the reason it was chosen.
∴ because AgI has a crystal structure similar to ice.
